system_prompt:
Return JSON only, exactly {"plans":[...]}. Plan numerical refinement, never layer JSON. Each plan has parent_design_id, action (refine_family or refine_layers), diagnosis (diagnosis_id, observation_ids, explanation citing concrete measured changes), expected_goal_changes (every original objective_id mapped to increase/decrease/unchanged/unknown). Use supplied short parent_alias P001 etc as parent_design_id, and diagnosis_alias D001 etc as diagnosis_id. Choose only supplied certified parents. Preserve all original objectives and physical conditions. refine_family preserves shared variables; refine_layers explicitly creates independent layer variables within original family bounds. Expectations are untested, not outcomes. No route or plan-count ceiling. Interpret measurements, local derivative arithmetic, and hypotheses separately. For a decreasing variable reverse the derivative sign; respect each goal sense and the supplied bounds. Local directional estimates do not establish finite-step outcomes or a unique mechanism. Explain why the chosen parent and action are informative; nearby parents need a reason, not a diversity quota. Exploratory actions, predicted tradeoffs, and unsuccessful hypotheses are legitimate; do not promise improvement. An empty plans list is allowed. Do not fabricate observations, material identities or new bounds.
Review the actual branch feedback before proposing the next coarse plans. Explain which observations support continuing, broadening, or changing a hypothesis. Different opinions and speculative interpretations are allowed. Separate the model-proposed seed from subsequent numerical refinement. Cached rediscoveries are not independent new experiments. Failure within a finite search budget does not disprove a hypothesis. These next plans remain unexecuted; do not claim new outcomes.

task_sheet.original_question: 我正在为多光谱成像相机设计一片可见-近红外双波段分光膜。要求可见光波段 450-650 nm 尽可能高的反射率（用于 RGB 通道成像），同时近红外波段 700-1000 nm 尽可能高的透过率（用于 NIR 通道）。请在 45 度入射、熔融石英基底条件下，仅使用 TiO2 和 SiO2 设计一个平面多层介质膜，膜系总层数不超过 24 层。采用非偏振光（s、p 偏振等权平均）；各波段目标均定义为按波长积分后除以波段宽度的平均值。
task_sheet.user_objective: Design a planar TiO2/SiO2 visible–NIR dichroic multilayer coating for multispectral imaging, maximizing wavelength-integral mean RGB reflectance and NIR transmittance at 45 degrees with equal-s/p unpolarized light under the stated constraints.

goal_relationships.coupling: G1 and G2 are distinct spectral goals for the same coating and may be physically coupled or trade off; their priority, weighting and acceptable compromise are unspecified.

explicit_constraints.constraint: Only TiO2 and SiO2 coating materials
explicit_constraints.original_span: 仅使用 TiO2 和 SiO2
膜系总层数不超过 24 层

explicit_constraints.constraint: Unpolarized light with equal s/p weights
explicit_constraints.original_span: 非偏振光（s、p 偏振等权平均）

explicit_constraints.constraint: Wavelength-integral band mean divided by band width
explicit_constraints.original_span: 各波段目标均定义为按波长积分后除以波段宽度的平均值

unknowns_assumptions.statement: Optical constants/dispersion, incident medium, fabrication tolerances and individual thickness bounds remain to be resolved before physical execution; this sheet only maps supported objective definitions.
Numerical acceptance thresholds and objective weights are unspecified; as high as possible is not 99%. No combined score is defined here.

candidate_mechanisms.mechanism: Interference in alternating high/low-index dielectric layers can form a visible stopband and NIR passband
Oblique-incidence optical phase and s/p admittance differences can shift/split spectral edges and affect leakage

assumptions.incident_medium: Demonstration configuration assumes air incidence; this is not an explicit statement in the user question and must be confirmed before physical execution.

route_rationales.claim: A standard quarter-wave stack centered at a blue-shifted visible wavelength will provide baseline visible reflection and NIR transmission at 45 degrees.
Thickening the high-index layers relative to low-index layers (non-quarter-wave) can broaden the stopband to cover the full visible range at 45 degrees.
route_rationales.model_knowledge_rationale: Quarter-wave stacks have symmetric stopbands; thickening the high-index layer breaks symmetry and can extend the long-wavelength edge of the stopband, which is useful if the 45-degree blue shift cuts off the red end of the visible spectrum.

route_rationales.claim: A model-knowledge hypothesis that matching the optical phase thickness of s and p polarizations via specific non-quarter-wave ratios reduces polarization leakage.
route_rationales.model_knowledge_rationale: Based on Fresnel equations, s and p admittances diverge at oblique angles. A quarter-wave stack optimized for normal incidence splits into two distinct bands at 45 degrees. By empirically tuning thicknesses (thickening H, thinning L or vice versa), one can attempt to overlap these bands or create a composite plateau that maximizes the unpolarized mean.

route_rationales.claim: Adding a matching layer or modifying the first/last layer thickness can reduce surface reflection losses in the NIR band, improving G2.
route_rationales.model_knowledge_rationale: While source D4 discusses AR coatings on separate surfaces, physical reasoning suggests the first layer of the stack itself can serve as a single-layer AR coating for the passband if its thickness is optimized independently of the quarter-wave condition of the rest of the stack.

route_rationales.claim: Optimizing the thickness of the first incident layer independently (non-quarter-wave) improves NIR transmission by acting as an AR layer.
route_rationales.model_knowledge_rationale: Physical reasoning based on single-layer AR coating principles: a layer with thickness d != lambda/4n can still minimize reflection if its effective admittance matches the geometric mean of incident and substrate admittances at the specific angle and wavelength.

route_rationales.claim: Increasing the total number of periods (up to the 24-layer limit) will maximize visible reflectance (G1) by increasing the stopband depth.
route_rationales.model_knowledge_rationale: While evidence supports more layers = higher reflectance, the specific thickness ratio adjustment for 45 degrees is a model-knowledge extrapolation to counteract angular blue-shift and polarization splitting in a deep stack.

route_rationales.claim: Model-knowledge route: Using a 'chirped' thickness profile (gradually changing layer thicknesses) can broaden the reflection band to cover the entire visible spectrum.
route_rationales.model_knowledge_rationale: Source mentions chirped stacks; physical reasoning dictates that a gradient in optical thickness maps to a gradient in central wavelength, effectively tiling the spectrum to widen the aggregate stopband.

decision_clues.physical_effect: Constructive interference creates a high-reflection band centered at the Bragg wavelength; increasing pair count narrows the band and increases reflectivity.
decision_clues.inference_bridge: Hypothesize that shifting the Bragg wavelength from NIR (950 nm) to visible (~550 nm) by reducing layer thicknesses will invert the spectral function to reflect visible and transmit NIR, subject to angular shift corrections.
conditions_and_unknowns: Source targets NIR reflection (950 nm) for shielding, whereas the task requires visible reflection and NIR transmission.
Normal incidence assumed in source formula; task requires 45 degrees.
No explicit polarization averaging details provided in snippet.

decision_clues.physical_effect: Blue shift of the reflection band center wavelength as incidence angle increases.
decision_clues.inference_bridge: Propose compensating for the 45-degree blue shift by designing the normal-incidence Bragg wavelength slightly longer than the target visible center, ensuring the shifted band aligns with 450-650 nm at the operating angle.
conditions_and_unknowns: Quantitative shift magnitude (110 nm) cited for 0 to 60 degrees; exact shift at 45 degrees for TiO2/SiO2 is not explicitly calculated in text.
Polarization splitting effects mentioned generally but not quantified for this specific material pair in the snippet.

decision_clues.physical_effect: Steep transition between reflection and transmission bands.
decision_clues.inference_bridge: Use the concept of a sharp edge filter but relocate the crossover point to the 650-700 nm gap by adjusting optical thicknesses, aiming for a similarly narrow transition zone.
conditions_and_unknowns: Source cutoff is at 950 nm (reflecting VIS+NIR up to 950); task requires cutoff between 650 and 700 nm.
Substrate and angle specifics for this quote are not fully detailed in the snippet excerpt.

diagnosis.explanation: Design P075 achieved a significant G1 increase (+0.015) by boosting blue and red subband reflectance, but suffered a catastrophic G2 loss (-0.193) across all NIR subbands. Local derivatives for layer_2:dH suggest a potential common ascent direction for both goals if increased, while layer_10:dH and layer_9:dL show strong negative impact on G2. The tradeoff indicates the current thickness profile creates excessive reflection in the NIR passband.

Design P056 demonstrates a massive G2 gain (+0.150) compared to baseline P053, with uniform improvement across all NIR subbands and polarizations. However, this came at the cost of G1 (-0.036), primarily due to a severe drop in the blue visible subband (-0.124). Local derivatives indicate layer_0:dH is at its lower bound (40nm) and increasing it improves G1 but hurts G2, highlighting a sharp spectral edge conflict.

Compared to baseline P048, P002 shows modest simultaneous improvements in G1 (+0.004) and G2 (+0.028). The G1 gain is driven by the red subband (+0.023) despite losses in blue and middle visible bands. G2 improved uniformly across NIR. Local derivatives suggest increasing dH improves G1 but degrades G2, while dL changes have mixed effects, indicating the shared variable parameterization limits independent spectral control.

Design P001 exhibits a strong G2 gain (+0.140) with uniform NIR improvement, but a notable G1 loss (-0.023). The G1 loss is concentrated in the blue subband (-0.199), while the red subband actually gained (+0.138). This suggests the chirped or varied thickness profile in family F004 has shifted the stopband too far red or narrowed it, failing to cover the blue end of the visible spectrum at 45 degrees.

P004 represents a high-G1 (0.895) but moderate-G2 (0.818) design. Local derivatives show that specific high-index layers (layer_0, layer_10) strongly negatively impact G2 when thickened, while other high-index layers (layer_4, 6, 8) have weak positive effects on G1. The lack of a joint ascent direction in the saved data suggests that independent layer adjustments are required to decouple the visible stopband depth from NIR leakage.

branches.rationale: Hypothesis: The catastrophic G2 loss in P075 is driven by excessive reflection from the deepest high-index layers (L10) and the interface layer (L0). This branch tests a 'front-loaded' strategy: slightly thickening L0 and L2 to sharpen the visible band edge while thinning L10 to reduce NIR leakage, aiming to recover G2 without sacrificing the G1 gains.

Counter-hypothesis to br_001: The NIR leakage is caused by the low-index matching layers (L9, L11) being too thick, creating constructive interference for reflection in the NIR. This branch aggressively thins the final three layers to disrupt the NIR stopband formation while maintaining the core stack thickness for visible reflection.

P056 has perfect G2 but failed G1 due to the blue drop. Since L0 is at its lower bound (40nm), this branch tests a minimal increase (to 48nm) coupled with a compensatory decrease in L10 (the other critical high-index layer) to maintain the NIR transmission window. It explores if a slight shift in the short-wavelength cutoff can be tolerated to regain blue reflectance.

Tests a linear chirp hypothesis where layer thicknesses gradually decrease from the substrate towards the air interface (or vice versa) to broaden the reflection band. P056's extreme values suggest a non-linear profile is needed; this branch imposes a smoother gradient on the high-index layers to cover the 450-650nm range more uniformly without closing the NIR window.

P002 showed modest simultaneous gains but is limited by the shared variable constraint. This branch tests the hypothesis that increasing the high-index thickness (dH) shifts the stopband redward (helping red/G1) while decreasing dL might compensate for NIR leakage. It seeks the 'sweet spot' where the stopband center aligns perfectly with 550nm.

Alternative to br_005: Hypothesizes that maximizing the optical thickness of both layers pushes the higher-order harmonics further into the IR, potentially cleaning up the NIR tail while widening the fundamental stopband for better visible coverage. Tests the limits of the [50,80] and [70,120] bounds.

P001 failed in the blue subband. This branch specifically targets the first few layers (dH1, dL1) which control the short-wavelength edge. By thickening the initial high-index layer and adjusting the subsequent low-index layer, we aim to extend the reflection band down to 450nm without altering the deeper layers that ensure high NIR transmission.

Since P001 already had good red performance, this branch focuses on stabilizing the middle-visible region (500-550nm) by tweaking the central layers (dH3, dL3). The hypothesis is that the 'dip' in the visible spectrum is caused by a mismatch in the optical thickness ratio of the middle pairs, not the edges.

P004 is a periodic stack with moderate G2. This branch introduces a specific perturbation pattern: alternating slightly thicker and thinner high-index layers to create a mini-stopband structure that might suppress side-lobes in the NIR while maintaining the main visible peak. Tests sensitivity to small deviations from periodicity.

Complementary to br_009, this branch perturbs the low-index layers instead. The hypothesis is that modulating the spacer thickness (SiO2) is more effective at controlling the NIR transmission ripple than modulating the reflector thickness (TiO2), allowing for a cleaner passband.

Tests the 'matching layer' hypothesis. Keeps the bulk of the stack periodic (optimal for G1) but drastically changes only the first two layers to act as an anti-reflection coating for the NIR band. If successful, this proves that G1 and G2 can be decoupled by treating the surface layers differently from the bulk mirror.
